summary: For ages 8-9, learners decide which graph type fits which data type and read time graphs both at and between plotted points. Discrete data (counted, separate categories) belong in a bar chart with gaps between bars; continuous data are measured quantities, and when a measurement changes over time (temperature through a day, plant height over weeks) it fits a time/line graph whose points are joined because real values exist between them. Three load-bearing ideas: (1) the discrete/continuous distinction drives the choice of representation, (2) a joined line gives estimated values BETWEEN the plotted points (interpolation), which assumes the quantity changed fairly steadily between readings, and (3) the vertical scale must be read before judging how big a change is. Teaching contrasts the two graph types on related real data and reads time graphs at AND between points.
misconceptions: Chooses the wrong representation for the data type — separate bars for continuous time data, or joins discrete category bars into a line
Believes a time graph only tells us the values at the plotted points, not in between (misses continuity)
Reads a steep line as a big change without checking the vertical scale (misleading-scale effect)
Reads the shape of the line as a literal picture of the situation rather than as values against axes

activities.title: Dual-view grapher: choose the graph that fits the data
steps: Take a data set and choose whether to show it as separated bars or a joined line.
For 'favourite pets' (counted categories, e.g. cats and dogs) choose bars with gaps; for 'classroom temperature through the day' choose a joined line.
When tempted to join category values, ask yourself: 'what would a point BETWEEN cats and dogs mean?' and notice there is no sensible answer.
For the temperature line, drag a vertical guide to estimate the value at a time that was never actually recorded, e.g. 10:30, between the plotted points.
Say out loud why the line makes sense for temperature but not for pet categories, using the words discrete and continuous.
activities.insight: A joined line only makes sense when in-between values are real — that is exactly what continuous data means; counted categories have no in-between, so they go in separated bars.

activities.title: Check the scale before calling a change 'big'
steps: Look at a temperature line that appears steep and, before describing the change, read the numbers on the vertical axis.
Compare the same temperature data drawn on a stretched (widely spaced) vertical axis and on a compressed one; notice the line looks dramatic or gentle while the data is identical.
Optionally use a scale slider that stretches or shrinks the vertical axis of the same data to feel how the apparent size of the change changes.
State the actual size of the change in degrees, not just 'huge' from the steepness.
activities.insight: Steepness alone is misleading: the spacing of the vertical scale changes how big a change looks, so you must read the scale before judging the size of a change.

activities.title: Interpret a real time graph at and between points
steps: Read a time graph of classroom temperature through one day: state the temperature at a marked time, and estimate it at an unmarked time such as 10:30 by reading between points.
Describe what a falling section after 3pm tells you about the situation (temperature getting cooler over time).
Then take a table of how many children chose each of four fruits and decide which graph to draw; draw separated bars against an even scale.
Explain in words why a joined line is right for temperature but a bar chart is right for the fruit choices.
activities.insight: Interpreting continuous data means estimating values between points and reading rising/falling as change over time; choosing bars for discrete categories and lines for measured-over-time shows the data type drives the representation.

activities.title: Annotated time graph as a reference scaffold
steps: Tap parts of a static, annotated time graph to reveal what the axes, points and line mean.
Use it to recall the labels for a plotted point, the joined line (continuous change), and the vertical scale.
activities.insight: A labelled time graph helps name the parts, but as a fixed image it does not give a draggable, precise read-out at an unmarked time or let you restretch the vertical scale; a learner can still estimate a value between points by eye, while an interactive graph makes reading any time and testing scale effects directly manipulable.

checkQuestion: First: here is a time graph of the temperature in our classroom through one day — what was the temperature at 10:30, and what does the falling part after 3pm tell us? Then: here is a table of how many children chose each of four fruits — which kind of graph should you draw for THIS data, and draw it.
checkAnswer: Interpreting: reads 10:30 by going BETWEEN the plotted points (interpolating) and reads the falling section as the temperature getting cooler over time. Translating: chooses a BAR chart for the discrete fruit categories (separated bars) — not a line — and draws it against an even scale.
